title: RSI / Airway
subtitle: Preoxygenation, intubation, and failed-airway setup
inKit: ETT 7.0-7.5 for most adults, 8.0 for large males. Test the cuff.
Malleable stylet, pre-shaped: hockey stick or gentle curve
10 mL syringe for the cuff and a cuff manometer: 20-30 cmH2O
Laryngoscope handle, Mac 3 and Mac 4 blades. Check the light before the patient arrives.
Water-soluble or lidocaine lubricant for stylet tip and distal ETT
Bite block or sized oral airway
outsideKit: Video laryngoscope at the bedside before the paralytic
BVM with PEEP valve and O2 reservoir
Nasal cannula at 15 L/min for apneic oxygenation during laryngoscopy
Yankauer suction on, tested, at the right side of the head
Continuous waveform capnography. Colorimetric alone is not enough.
RSI drugs: induction agent and paralytic drawn, labeled, dose read aloud
Post-intubation sedation ready before the paralytic: propofol, ketamine, or fentanyl plus midazolam infusion
Push-dose epinephrine drawn and labeled. Norepinephrine running or ready if hypotensive before induction.
Ventilator set: TV 6-8 mL/kg IBW, FiO2 100%, PEEP 5, rate 14. Metabolic acidosis: match the pre-intubation minute ventilation.
Cardiac monitor
commonlyForgotten: Nasal cannula left on under the BVM during laryngoscopy
PEEP valve on the BVM before preoxygenation
Waveform capnography. Colorimetric can read falsely negative in low-flow states and cardiac arrest.
Suction on before the first bag-mask breath
Post-intubation sedation drawn and labeled. The induction agent wears off in minutes. Rocuronium paralysis lasts 45 min or more.
Second ETT, one size smaller
patientSetup: Ramp until the external auditory meatus is level with the sternal notch, especially in obesity and pregnancy: blankets, ramp pillow or scoop
Bed at the intubator's standing working height
IV patent on flush before any medication
Monitoring: waveform SpO2, waveform ETCO2, BP every 2 min, cardiac telemetry
Roles assigned before induction: BVM, drugs, cricoid if used. Brief them aloud.
Say the plan before the paralytic: primary airway, backup device, surgical rescue
sterileSetup: Clean technique, clean gloves
Keep the distal 10 cm of the ETT and the cuff uncontaminated
Mayo stand: ETT and stylet shaped, syringe on, lubricant applied. Blade on, light checked.
Backup blade (different size or video) on the Mayo stand or within reach
Yankauer uncapped at the right side of the head before induction
backupEquipment: Bougie (Eschmann stylet) in hand or on the Mayo stand. Use it at the first difficult view. Never blind at a grade 3-4 view.
Video laryngoscope in the room before the paralytic is given
Second-generation supraglottic airway (i-gel): rescue oxygenation after failed intubation, before front-of-neck access
Surgical airway kit (cric tray) in the room before RSI begins. Indication is CICO.
Difficult airway cart location known to everyone in the room before induction begins
references: Brown CA 3rd, Sakles JC, Mick NW, eds. The Walls Manual of Emergency Airway Management, 5th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2018.
Brown CA 3rd, Bair AE, Pallin DJ, Walls RM; NEAR III Investigators. Techniques, success, and adverse events of emergency department adult intubations. Ann Emerg Med. 2015;65(4):363-370.e1.
Weingart SD, Levitan RM. Preoxygenation and prevention of desaturation during emergency airway management. Ann Emerg Med. 2012;59(3):165–175.
American College of Emergency Physicians. Clinical Policy: Critical Issues in the Management of Adult Patients Requiring Endotracheal Intubation in the Emergency Department. 2025.

title: Surgical Airway (Cric)
subtitle: Can't intubate, can't oxygenate: front-of-neck access
inKit: 6.0 cuffed ETT or 6.0 cuffed cric tube
10 mL syringe, pre-charged with air on the field for cuff inflation
Cloth tape or suture to secure the tube
outsideKit: Suction on at the bedside
BVM on O2, to ventilate through the tube once it is in
Waveform capnography
Headlamp or procedure light. Overhead light alone is not enough.
Second person keeps oxygenating from above (facemask or SGA) while you cut. Trauma: another person for manual in-line stabilization. The operator's non-dominant hand holds the larynx.
commonlyForgotten: Headlamp
Suction before you cut
Bougie through the membrane before the tube
Confirm with waveform capnography, not colorimetric. Low-output states give false negatives.
Impalpable membrane: vertical skin incision first, then a horizontal stab through the membrane
Full neuromuscular block before the incision
6.0 ETT: advance until the cuff is just past the membrane, then 1-2 cm more. At its usual 21 cm mark it is in the right main bronchus.
patientSetup: Shoulder roll to extend the neck. Trauma: no roll, neutral with inline stabilization.
Landmarks before cutting: thyroid notch, then down the midline to the soft space of the cricothyroid membrane
Larynx stabilized: non-dominant thumb and middle finger on the thyroid cartilage, index finger on the membrane
Right-handed operator on the patient's right
Semi-elective: mark the membrane with a skin marker. Emergency: finger stabilization.
Remove neck jewelry. Loosen the collar or cervical collar before prep.
sterileSetup: Betadine or chlorhexidine over the anterior neck if time permits. In CICO: clean gloves and proceed immediately.
Sterile drape if time permits
Mayo stand: scalpel, bougie, tube and syringe, hook if used, suction, gauze
Suction next to the working field
backupEquipment: Needle (cannula) cricothyrotomy: children under 8-10 only. Adults: scalpel-bougie-tube.
Commercial Seldinger cric kit: only if that is what is stocked. Follow its instructions. Otherwise scalpel-bougie-tube.
references: Brown CA 3rd, Sakles JC, Mick NW, eds. The Walls Manual of Emergency Airway Management, 5th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2018.

Ahmad I, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. 2026;136(1):283-307. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.10.006

title: Central Venous Catheter
subtitle: Triple-lumen CVC: IJ, subclavian, or femoral under ultrasound
inKit: Triple-lumen CVC: 15-16 cm right IJ or subclavian, 20 cm left-sided or femoral
Guidewire, J-tip 0.035". Track the depth mark at the skin throughout.
Scalpel, #11 blade, for the skin nick
10 mL syringe for aspiration and flushing
Large sterile drapes and fenestrated drape
3-0 silk on a straight needle, or StatLock
Transparent occlusive dressing, with or without Biopatch
outsideKit: Ultrasound, linear probe 10-15 MHz
Sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Sterile gown
Extra chlorhexidine applicators. One kit stick is not enough.
Cardiac monitor during wire passage. Ectopy means the wire is in the RV: pull back.
10 mL saline flushes ×3, one per lumen
IJ or subclavian: chest X-ray for tip at the cavoatrial junction and pneumothorax
Blood culture bottles if drawing cultures at placement
Sterile extension tubing for manometry
commonlyForgotten: Sterile probe cover and sterile gel. Non-sterile gel does not substitute.
Mark the wire depth at the skin before dilating
Wire in the vein on ultrasound in two planes before the dilator passes. Not clearly seen: manometry.
All lumens primed with saline, and every port except the wire port capped, before the catheter goes in
IJ or subclavian: chest X-ray reviewed before use where policy requires. Resuscitation drugs do not wait for it.
Wire out, intact, held up and said aloud before the dressing
patientSetup: IJ: Trendelenburg 15-20 degrees, head slightly turned away (avoid over-rotation), roll under the ipsilateral shoulder
Subclavian: roll under the scapulae (not mid-back), arm tucked at the side, slight Trendelenburg
Femoral: leg extended and externally rotated, table flat
Time-out before draping: patient ID, site, side, allergies (especially chlorhexidine), procedure
Maximal barrier precautions: cap, mask with eye protection, sterile gown, sterile gloves
Non-sterile assistant for ultrasound, medications, specimen tubes, sharps
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine back-and-forth scrub, 30 seconds (2 minutes at the groin). Full 2 minutes to dry.
Betadine if chlorhexidine allergy, 2 minutes to dry
Sterile drape head to toe, fenestrated over the site
Mayo stand in order: catheter primed and capped except the wire port, lidocaine syringe, introducer needle, guidewire, scalpel, dilator
Sterile probe cover on before skin puncture. No scanning without it.
backupEquipment: Introducer sheath (Cordis): if 8.5 Fr large-bore access is needed for resuscitation, emergent RHC, or transvenous pacer passage
Dialysis catheter (Vas-Cath): if CRRT or acute hemodialysis is anticipated
Two large-bore peripheral IVs as bridge if central access is delayed
Arterial line if continuous hemodynamic monitoring is simultaneously required
references: McGee DC, Gould MK. Preventing Complications of Central Venous Catheterization. N Engl J Med. 2003;348:1123–1133.
Buetti N, Marschall J, Drees M, et al. Strategies to prevent central line-associated bloodstream infections in acute-care hospitals: 2022 Update. Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol. 2022;43(5):553-569.
Hind D, et al. Ultrasonic locating devices for central venous cannulation: meta-analysis. BMJ. 2003;327:361.
O'Grady NP, et al. Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections. CDC/HICPAC 2011.

title: Chest Tube / Thoracostomy
subtitle: Large-bore drainage for hemothorax, unstable trauma, or a large air leak
inKit: Chest tube sized to indication: 28-32 Fr for significant hemothorax, unstable trauma, or a large air leak, ventilated or not. Choose before opening.
Large curved Kelly clamps ×2: one to dissect, one to pass the tube
Scalpel, #10 blade, or #21 for a large incision
20 mL syringe, 25g and 22g needles for lidocaine
0 silk or 0 Prolene on a large curved needle for anchoring
Petroleum gauze (Xeroform) for the exit site
Silk or cloth tape for anchoring
outsideKit: Pleural drainage system (e.g. Pleur-evac), water seal filled with sterile water before connecting
Sterile connector tubing, chest tube to drainage system
Wall suction available for the drainage system, -20 cmH2O if prescribed
Lidocaine 1%, up to 3 mg/kg to 250 mg for pleural infiltration (about 20 mL at 70 kg). Most kits hold only 10 mL.
IV morphine or fentanyl
Chest X-ray right after placement for tube position
Pulse oximetry and cardiac monitor through the procedure and recovery
Non-sterile assistant for tubing, drainage system, suction
Large hemothorax, hypotensive: blood at the bedside and a surgeon aware before draining
Adult trauma: one dose of a first-generation cephalosporin at insertion
commonlyForgotten: Drainage system filled to the water-seal line before connecting
Petroleum gauze at the exit site
Adequate analgesia before the incision
After connecting: water seal oscillating. Suction only if prescribed.
Horizontal mattress anchor suture. Tape alone is not enough.
patientSetup: Ipsilateral arm above the head (hand behind the head or draped overhead)
Safe triangle: lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, nipple line (5th ICS) inferiorly, apex below the axilla
Mark the site before prep when possible
Alert patient: head of bed 30-45°
IV opioid 5-10 min before prep. Local at the site with a rib periosteum block.
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine axilla to midline, 3 complete passes, 2 min to dry
Sterile drape, neck to waist
Sterile gown and gloves, mask, eye protection
Mayo stand in order: lidocaine syringe, scalpel, clamps ×2, chest tube (distal end clamped), suture, petroleum gauze
backupEquipment: Pigtail catheter (Seldinger kit): 8-14 Fr uncomplicated pneumothorax, 12-14 Fr free-flowing effusion, when a large-bore tube is not indicated

Needle decompression for tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic compromise: 14g or larger, at least 8 cm, 4th or 5th ICS anterior axillary line, alternate 2nd ICS midclavicular. In arrest, do not wait for the chest tube.
Surgery or trauma now: 1,500 mL on insertion, more than 200 mL/h for 3 hours, or instability with ongoing output
references: Dev SP, Nascimento B Jr, Simone C, Chien V. Chest-Tube Insertion. N Engl J Med. 2007;357:e15.
Mowery NT, et al. EAST Practice Management Guidelines for Management of Hemothorax and Occult Pneumothorax. J Trauma. 2011;70(2):510–518.
British Thoracic Society. Clinical Statement on pleural procedures. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s43-s68.

title: Arterial Line
subtitle: Radial A-line: continuous hemodynamic monitoring and ABG access
inKit: 20g arterial catheter-over-needle, 2-inch for obese or edematous wrists
outsideKit: Pressure transducer tubing kit, ordered separately
Pressure bag: 500 mL NS at 300 mmHg, tubing primed with no air bubbles
Transducer holder, pole or arm mount
Wrist roll: rolled gauze or folded towel
Cloth tape to hold the wrist extended
Monitor with the arterial channel selected and scaled
Transducer zeroed at the phlebostatic axis (4th ICS, mid-axillary line) before the line goes in
Ultrasound, linear probe, sterile probe cover and sterile gel
commonlyForgotten: Wrist extended 20-30° before prep
Tubing primed and transducer zeroed before the catheter goes in
Suture or StatLock. Tape alone is not enough.
Arterial waveform with a dicrotic notch before the dressing
Collateral flow checked on ultrasound before committing to the radial
patientSetup: Awake, cooperative patient: non-dominant wrist preferred
Wrist extended 20-30° over the roll. Tape the index, middle and ring fingers back without occluding circulation.
Radial pulse 1-2 cm proximal to the flexor wrist crease. Mark it with a thumbnail.
Arm at or below heart level
Ultrasound: linear probe 10-15 MHz, transverse over the radial artery
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine over the wrist. Let it dry.
Sterile mini-drape or towel over the wrist
Cap, mask and sterile gloves
Mayo stand: catheter assembled, syringe attached, dressing open
Primed, zeroed pressure tubing handed onto the field before the catheter goes in
backupEquipment: Femoral artery: if bilateral radial access fails. Full barrier precautions. Higher infection risk, and a puncture above the inguinal ligament cannot be compressed.
Brachial artery approach: end artery. Use only as a last resort because of hand ischemia risk.
NIBP cycling every 1 min as a bridge while arterial access is established
references: Scheer BV, Perel A, Pfeiffer UJ. Clinical review: Complications and risk factors of peripheral arterial catheters used for hemodynamic monitoring. Crit Care. 2002;6(3):199–204.
Brzezinski M, Luisetti T, London MJ. Radial artery cannulation: a comprehensive review of recent anatomic and physiologic investigations. Anesth Analg. 2009;109(6):1763–1781.
Slogoff S, Keats AS, Arlund C. On the safety of radial artery cannulation. Anesthesiology. 1983;59(1):42–47.

title: Lumbar Puncture
subtitle: CSF sampling for meningitis, SAH workup, and ICP measurement
inKit: Spinal needle: 22-25g Sprotte/Whitacre pencil-point with its introducer, the default for adults. Less post-LP headache, harder first pass.
Stylet in while the needle advances. Take it out every few millimeters to check for flow.
1% lidocaine, 10 mL syringe, 25g and 22g needles for skin and deep infiltration
outsideKit: Ultrasound, curvilinear probe (linear in thin patients), to find the midline and interspace in obese, elderly or scoliotic patients
Fluoroscopy (IR) if bedside attempts fail
Labs ordered before starting: cell count (tubes 1 and 4), glucose, protein, Gram stain and culture. Xanthochromia if SAH suspected.
Extra tubes for cytology, TB, fungal antigen or unusual studies: 3-8 mL more
Non-sterile assistant to hold the patient flexed and pass tubes without touching the field
commonlyForgotten: All 4 tubes labeled before opening the kit
Opening pressure in lateral decubitus, legs relaxed, before removing any CSF. Closing pressure too.
Stylet back in before withdrawing the needle
Cell count on tube 4 as well as tube 1: RBCs falling from tube 1 to 4 suggest a traumatic tap but do not exclude SAH
Chlorhexidine fully dry before the spinal needle. Wet chlorhexidine is neurotoxic.
Suspected bacterial meningitis: blood cultures and antibiotics before the kit is opened. Blood glucose just before the LP.
patientSetup: Lateral decubitus: knees to chest, chin tucked, back arched toward the operator. A pillow between the knees keeps the spine horizontal.
Or seated, leaning forward over a pillow on the bedside table, arms crossed and supported. Better spinal flexion in obese patients.
L3-L4 or L4-L5. The iliac crests are at about the L4 spinous process.
Mark the interspace with a thumbnail indent before prep
Lateral decubitus: operator seated, bed at working height
Assistant holds the patient flexed. Movement during needle passage risks a bloody tap.
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine in widening circles ×3. Full 2 minutes to dry before the spinal needle.
Sterile drapes, fenestrated over the interspace
Sterile gloves and mask
In order: lidocaine syringe, exploring needle, spinal needle, stopcock and manometer, tubes
Cutting needle only: bevel parallel to the dural fibers (facing the flank in lateral position)
backupEquipment: Ultrasound-guided approach: use when bony landmarks are not palpable. Mark the interspace with the probe before prepping.
Fluoroscopy-guided LP (IR): for severe obesity, scoliosis, prior lumbar surgery, or multiple failed bedside attempts
20g Quincke cutting needle: the fallback when no atraumatic needle is stocked. Higher post-LP headache incidence.
Blood patch (anesthesia consult): for post-LP headache that does not resolve with caffeine and supine positioning
Longer spinal needle (5 in / 127 mm) for large body habitus
references: Straus SE, Thorpe KE, Holroyd-Leduc J. How do I perform a lumbar puncture and analyze the results to diagnose bacterial meningitis? JAMA. 2006;296(16):2012–2022.
van Crevel H, Hijdra A, de Gans J. Lumbar puncture and the risk of herniation: when should we first perform CT? J Neurol. 2002;249(2):129–137.
Armon C, Evans RW; Therapeutics and Technology Assessment Subcommittee. Addendum to assessment: prevention of post-lumbar puncture headaches. Neurology. 2005;65(4):510–512.

title: Thoracentesis
subtitle: Pleural fluid sampling or therapeutic drainage under ultrasound guidance
inKit: Catheter-over-needle thoracentesis assembly, 8-9 cm, side holes
Drainage bag (1000-1500 mL) for gravity drainage, or syringe and stopcock
1% lidocaine, 10 mL syringe, 25g and 22g needles. Infiltrate generously to the parietal pleura.
10 mL and 20 mL syringes for aspiration
outsideKit: Ultrasound, curvilinear 3.5-5 MHz
Sterile probe cover for real-time needle guidance
Lab tubes, ordered before starting: LDH, protein, glucose, cell count, Gram stain and culture, cytology
Heparinized syringe for pleural fluid pH if parapneumonic effusion suspected
Chest X-ray or ultrasound after the procedure for pneumothorax
Pulse oximetry and cardiac monitor during and for 1 hour after
Non-sterile assistant to hold the patient seated and pass specimen containers
commonlyForgotten: Mark with ultrasound immediately before the procedure. Not hours earlier, and not before a position change.
No more than 1000-1500 mL at one sitting (re-expansion pulmonary edema)
Needle over the top of the rib. The neurovascular bundle runs along the inferior margin.
pH in suspected parapneumonic effusion: below 7.20 needs tube drainage, not just sampling
Bevel down, away from the lung, during aspiration to reduce pneumothorax risk
patientSetup: Seated, leaning forward onto a pillow on the overbed table
Arms crossed and supported to move the scapulae out of the way
Posterior-lateral approach at the deepest pocket on ultrasound, not below the 9th rib
Skin-mark right after scanning. Thumbnail indent as a second reference.
Cannot sit up: supine, ipsilateral arm overhead, mid-axillary approach
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine ×3 passes over the marked site, posterior-lateral chest (lateral if supine). 2 minutes to dry.
Large sterile drape, fenestrated over the site
Sterile gloves and mask
Mayo stand in order: lidocaine syringe, exploring needle, thoracentesis catheter, collection tubing, drainage bag
Drainage bag below the patient before aspiration begins
backupEquipment: Pigtail catheter (12-14 Fr Seldinger kit): for drainage over days. Loculated effusion: image-guided or specialist placement.
Empyema or frank pus: 14 Fr or smaller drain with scheduled flushes. Large-bore chest tube only if a small-bore drain has failed.
Needle decompression: if tension pneumothorax develops with acute hemodynamic compromise post-procedure
references: Gordon CE, Feller-Kopman D, Balk EM, Smetana GW. Pneumothorax following thoracentesis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Arch Intern Med. 2010;170(4):332–339.
British Thoracic Society. Clinical Statement on pleural procedures. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s43-s68.
Light RW. Parapneumonic effusions and empyema. Proc Am Thorac Soc. 2006;3(1):75–80.
ACCP Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis and Management of Lung Cancer, 3rd ed. Pleural Effusion section. 2013.

title: Pericardiocentesis
subtitle: Emergency relief of pericardial tamponade under echo guidance
inKit: Pericardiocentesis needle: 18g spinal, 6-9 cm, or commercial kit
Seldinger kit: 0.035" J-tip guidewire, dilator, pigtail or straight drainage catheter
Agitated saline: 10 mL saline, two 10 mL syringes and a second three-way stopcock
outsideKit: Bedside echo, phased-array or curvilinear 2-5 MHz: effusion size and approach window
Sterile probe cover for real-time echo guidance
Continuous cardiac monitor with rhythm strip throughout
Crash cart at the bedside: pads on, defibrillator ready, epinephrine 1 mg and atropine 1 mg drawn
Cardiothoracic surgery aware before starting. A surgical pericardial window may be needed if drainage fails.
Continuous BP, pulse oximetry and waveform. Two running IVs.
Sterile pressure tubing to the transducer, to confirm the tip is not in the ventricle
commonlyForgotten: Echo before the needle: effusion location, size and approach. This avoids RV free-wall puncture.
After stabilization, stage the drainage: under about 500 mL at first, then at intervals (pericardial decompression syndrome)
Seldinger kit: leave the drain in until output falls below about 25-30 mL/day. Malignant effusions recur within hours.
Brisk clotting supports intracardiac blood but is not proof. Confirm with agitated saline, the needle seen in the space, or a transduced waveform.
Wire seen inside the pericardial space on echo before dilating. No exception.
patientSetup: Head of bed 30-45 degrees
Choose the window on echo before prep: subxiphoid, parasternal or apical. Largest pocket, shortest safe path. Parasternal: internal mammary on color Doppler first.
Subxiphoid: 1 cm below the costal margin just left of the xiphoid, 30-45 degrees, toward the left shoulder
Apical: 5th-6th ICS just lateral to the left cardiac border, angled 30 degrees posteriorly and superiorly
Hemodynamically compromised: IV fluid bolus before drainage
Operator on the patient's right for subxiphoid, left for parasternal or apical
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine over the subxiphoid, parasternal or apical site, 2 min to dry. Peri-arrest: splash prep, gloves, and go. Do not wait for drying, drape or gown.
Sterile drapes
Sterile gloves, gown and mask
60 mL syringe on the stopcock at the needle hub before insertion
backupEquipment: Cardiothoracic surgery, not a needle, for aortic dissection, free-wall rupture, or a purulent or clotted effusion. Dissection or rupture with impending arrest and no surgeon: 10-20 mL aliquots only, to the lowest pressure that perfuses, then stop. Surgery also for trauma hemopericardium (needle only to bridge), failed bedside drainage, or loculated effusion.
Pericardiocentesis under fluoroscopy (cardiac cath lab): for difficult anatomy
Balloon pericardiotomy (IR): for recurrent malignant effusions that need a definitive window without open surgery
references: European Society of Cardiology. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Myocarditis and Pericarditis. Eur Heart J. 2025;46(40):3952. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192
Tsang TS, Freeman WK, Sinak LJ, Seward JB. Echocardiographically guided pericardiocentesis: evolution and state-of-the-art technique. Mayo Clin Proc. 1998;73(7):647–652.
Fitch MT, Nicks BA, Pariyadath M, McGinnis HD, Manthey DE. Emergency pericardiocentesis. N Engl J Med. 2012;366:e17.
